meaning: The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school

phonemes.desc: The canonical restored form Vasubandhu — a Sanskrit compound, not a Greek-accented name; the elements are vasu, 'wealth, good', and bandhu, 'kinsman, friend'.

pronunciation.approximation: Say "vasubandhu" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Vasubandhu".
pronunciation.note: The ASCII form "vasubandhu" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Vasubandhu" preserves the name's scholarly dignity. Sanskrit is not a stress-accent language like Greek; the name is a transparent compound of vasu ('wealth, good') + bandhu ('kinsman, friend') — 'Kinsman of Wealth' — so there is no distinctive accent or long-vowel mark for a restoration to recover, and the lexicon classifies the name Tier 2. What the capitals restore is recognition, not phonology.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: वसुबन्धु (vasubandhu), 'kinsman of wealth' — vasu 'wealth, good' + bandhu 'kinsman, friend' (Monier-Williams, s.v.)

kin.label: Pāli / Tibetan
kin.form: Vasubandhu in Pāli sources; Tibetan dbyig gnyen, the standard calque translating vasu as 'wealth' (dbyig) and bandhu as 'friend' (gnyen)

kin.label: Family names
kin.form: His mother was named Virañcī; his father Kauśika, a brahmin of Puruṣapura (Peshawar) — his elder half-brother was Asaṅga (Tibetan biographies)

domains.title: Vasubandhu
domains.subtitle: Abhidharma
domains.lead: Vasubandhu is the great systematizer of Buddhist philosophy: author of the Abhidharmakośa, the encyclopedia of Abhidharma that every later school had to answer, and, with his half-brother Asaṅga, co-founder of the Yogācāra, the 'Mind-Only' school that reshaped Mahāyāna thought from India to Japan.

cards.name: The Kośa Verse
cards.desc: Six hundred verses of Abhidharmakośa kārikā summarizing the entire Sarvāstivāda analysis of mind, matter, and liberation.

cards.name: Abhidharma
cards.desc: His auto-commentary made the Kośa the standard curriculum: studied in Nālandā, debated in Tibet, translated in China by Xuanzang.

cards.name: Yogācāra
cards.desc: The Twenty and Thirty Verses argue the world is 'mind-only' — the doctrine his Kośa-era Sautrāntika readers found hardest to accept.

cards.name: The Conversion
cards.desc: Legend says his brother Asaṅga sent him a begging letter: compassion, not argument, turned the Kośa's author toward the Mahāyāna.

symbols.name: The Kośa stanza
symbols.meaning: A verse (kārikā) whose eight-syllable lines hold whole Abhidharma treatises — scholarship compressed into memorable sound

symbols.name: The begging bowl
symbols.meaning: The monk's only equipment; Vasubandhu remained a bhikṣu all his life even while moving courts and schools

symbols.name: The letter from Asaṅga
symbols.meaning: In the Tibetan biographies, the note that converted him — affection and mortality doing what doctrine could not

symbols.name: Treasury (kośa)
symbols.meaning: The storehouse metaphor of the Abhidharmakośa: every dharma catalogued like treasure in a vault, each with its own nature

mythology.lead: Vasubandhu was a historical philosopher, not a mythological figure — a monk of Puruṣapura (Peshawar) who, the early Tibetan biographies say, wrote the Abhidharmakośa as a Sarvāstivādin critic and then embraced the Yogācāra Mahāyāna of his half-brother Asaṅga. His 'myths' are the legends his tradition grew around a real life.

myths.title: Three Years in Seclusion
myths.text: The Tibetan biographies recount that Vasubandhu withdrew into seclusion to master the Abhidharma of the Kashmir Sarvāstivādins, and emerged with the Abhidharmakośa — six hundred verses (kārikā) of flawless eight-syllable metre that summarized the entire system. When the Kashmir masters admired the verses but missed their own subtlety, he added an auto-commentary (bhāṣya) of his own in which, tradition says, he quietly refuted them. The Kośa became what it remains: the one Abhidharma text every later school — Theravāda, Mahāyāna, and the Tibetan lineages — had to study, debate, or answer, translated in its entirety into Chinese by Xuanzang and memorized in fragments by generations of monks from Kashmir to Kyoto. Its author's own allegiance was already drifting as he wrote: the commentary, tradition says, shows the Sautrāntika reservations that would later make his conversion credible. To condense a library into verse, and the verse into a single lifetime, is the legend's whole point: scholarship can be a kind of asceticism.

myths.title: The Begging Letter of Asaṅga
myths.text: Vasubandhu had mocked the Mahāyāna as a corruption of the Buddha's teaching, calling its scriptures fabrications. His elder half-brother Asaṅga, already a great Yogācāra teacher, sent him no rebuttal — only a note reporting that he was dying, and begging Vasubandhu to recite the Mahāyāna sūtras for him. Struck by the affection of the request, Vasubandhu read them, found them profound, and entered the Mahāyāna himself. The story is hagiography — no Indian source records it independently — yet it encodes the tradition's own account of its greatest conversion: Vasubandhu did not abandon analysis for devotion. He turned the same razor-sharp mind to the 'mind-only' philosophy, composing the Twenty Verses (Viṁśikā) and the Thirty Verses (Triṁśikā) that define the Yogācāra, and the two halves of his career became one continuous argument about how carefully the world must be taken apart before it can be seen whole.

myths.title: The Victory over Vasurāta
myths.text: The biographies carry Vasubandhu to the courts of northern India, where the grammarian-philosopher Vasurāta, champion of an opposing school, had humiliated all comers. Vasubandhu entered the contest — the tradition describes a great assembly of rival teachers and lay patrons gathered to watch — and his opponent was worsted. After the debate he was offered a great patron's gold — and the legends insist that, as a monk, he spent the wealth on works of benefit to the saṅgha and on gifts to the poor. The story matters less as history than as the template it sets: the philosopher's victory is measured not in refutation but in what the victor refuses to keep. Every medieval debate culture of the Buddhist world — Nālandā's, Tibet's, Japan's — repeated this scene with Vasubandhu's name in it, and his reputation as the undefeated champion of two successive orthodoxies made the later conversion legend necessary: only love, the tradition decided, could have beaten him.

myths.title: One Vasubandhu or Two?
myths.text: Modern scholarship has had to ask whether one man could have written both the Kośa's analytical Abhidharma and the Yogācāra's visionary metaphysics. Erich Frauwallner (1951) argued the dates fit a single long life; others have proposed two Vasubandhus — the Yogācāra co-founder and a later Kośa author — and the question is still argued in the journals. The tradition itself never doubted: one Vasubandhu, brother of Asaṅga, whose conversion joined the two oeuvres into a single career — and the hagiographies even extend that life into legend, saying he ended it in the Pure Land of Amitābha, or in Nepal, depending on which strand one follows. The modern debate is itself a tribute: few ancient authors are so prolific and so consistent in brilliance that posterity must ask whether they were two people.

lore.syncretism: Vasubandhu's legacy is the creation of a pan-Asian scholastic commons. In China, Xuanzang's pilgrimage was undertaken substantially to resolve disputes over the Kośa, and his massive translation of 649–660 CE made Vasubandhu the doctrinal backbone of the Faxiang (Consciousness-Only) school. In Japan the Hossō school of Nara claimed him as its patriarch, while the Kyoto lineages of the future would read his Viṁśikā as the foundation of 'mind-only' meditations. In Tibet every monastery curriculum begins with the Kośa. Modern comparative philosophy — from Thich Nhat Hanh's engaged Buddhism to analytic treatments of idealism — still frames its questions in his vocabulary. He is perhaps the only ancient philosopher whose works are simultaneously a living liturgy, a graduate textbook, and a modern research programme.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Abhidharmakośa never went out of use: it has been memorized, commented, and debated continuously for some fifteen centuries, from Nālandā to the great Tibetan commentarial traditions (Prajñākaramati's and Yaśomitra's subcommentaries in Sanskrit; Sthiramati's in the mind-only line). Its author is honored as a patriarch in China and Japan, and Tibetan debate courtyards still open with his verses. In the modern academy Vasubandhu anchors the study of Buddhist philosophy — his Viṁśikā is a standard text in courses on philosophy of mind, cited in debates about idealism and representation. A brahmin-born monk of Gandhāra thus became one of the most-read authors in human history, his name a byword for the possibility that analysis itself can be a path to compassion.
lore.extendedMeditation: Vasubandhu is the scholar as religious figure — proof that in the Buddhist world, thinking carefully was itself a sacred practice. His two careers look like a contradiction: the great classifier of the mind's parts, then the teacher who said the parts and the world they compose are 'mind-only'. Read together, they form one argument: you must take the world apart completely before you can see what holds it together. His legend conversion turns not on a vision but on a letter from a dying brother — intellect bending at last to love. Modern philosophy of mind still returns to his Viṁśikā, where a dream, a reflection, and the waking world are made to trade places in a few pages. Few ancient authors remain so contemporary: the question of what the world is made of, and whether mind is on the list, is still his question.

lore.archaeology: Vasubandhu left no shrine — his witnesses are manuscripts. Fragments of the Abhidharmakośa survive in Central Asian Sanskrit finds, and the complete tradition rides on Xuanzang's Chinese translation (Taishō 1558) and the later Tibetan canon (Toh. 4089–90). Gandhāra, his homeland, is one of the richest archaeological regions of the Buddhist world: the monastery and stupa complexes around Peshawar — where the biographies place his birth — have yielded the oldest datable Buddha images (c. 1st–3rd c. CE). At Nālandā, the university whose ruins still stand in Bihar, his Kośa was a founding text; the debate-court culture his legend describes is the same institution archaeology reveals. The colophons of the Dunhuang and Gilgit manuscript finds carry his name as authority across the Silk Road.
